synthesis: The block length K is a shared design variable: it fixes the number of outer blocks, determines how many Taylor-phase terms remain oscillatory and hence the degree and coefficient ranges of each local sum, and sets the lattice or precomputation size needed to evaluate those sums. The final exponent therefore comes from balancing global block count against coverage of the resulting evaluator parameter space.
source_support: The block decomposition gives about t^(1/2-beta) blocks when K is chosen at scale t^beta, while the Taylor truncation gives degree d=ceil(1/(1/2-beta))-1 and the coefficient ranges in Tables 1 and 2. The quadratic construction then explicitly balances precomputation cost C against P/K, and Theorem 2.2 supplies the K^(4mu) precomputation bound for the restricted cubic family.
nonparaphrase_operation: Connects the same scale parameter across three otherwise separate layers-local phase compression, evaluator parameter-space dimension, and end-to-end work-and identifies their balance as the mechanism selecting the complexity exponent.
limits: The balance is established for the paper's Riemann-Siegel block reduction and its stated quadratic or small-cubic evaluators. It is neither a general optimization principle nor a lower bound, and the asymptotic accounting does not establish practical constants.
quality_reason: Distinct parent units jointly provide the block-count/degree tradeoff, coefficient restrictions, and evaluator precomputation costs. No one parent alone supplies the full causal chain, and the synthesis preserves the conditional nature of the resulting exponents.

synthesis: Repeated Poisson or van der Corput shortening is progressive only after an intervention restores a usable representation: coefficients are normalized, and in the cubic case the nonpolynomial saddle phase is expanded so that sufficiently small higher-order terms can be removed while the retained phase remains cubic. The next iteration can then act on a shorter sum of essentially the same controlled type.
source_support: The introduction states that normalization between Poisson steps is precisely what prevents iteration from returning to its starting point. Section 3 normalizes the quadratic coefficient, expands the cubic saddle phase under |cK^2|<=0.01b and bK>=1, removes quartic and higher contributions with a short Taylor expansion, obtains the transformed cubic parameters in (3.13), and states that repeated applications yield sums of length at most K/2^m+2 while the conditions continue to hold.
nonparaphrase_operation: Identifies normalization and tail elimination as closure-restoring transformations that make length reduction composable, rather than treating the transform itself as sufficient progress.
limits: The cubic closure requires the stated small-coefficient, normalization, and stopping inequalities. When they fail, the algorithm exits to boundary evaluation or one final high-degree transform backed by precomputation; no unrestricted closure claim is supported.
quality_reason: The general intervention claim and the detailed cubic mechanism occur in distinct parent units and agree at the level of an explicit iterative dependency. The synthesis retains both the length reduction and the conditions under which the representation class is restored.

synthesis: The stopping cases are constituent branches of the cubic algorithm. Small length permits direct summation, weak quadratic curvature permits Euler-Maclaurin reduction, continued normalized curvature permits quadratic descent, stationary mass is deferred to saddle analysis, and loss of the small-cubic condition routes the terminal high-degree family to precomputed evaluation. Efficiency comes from matching each failed invariant to a different evaluator.
source_support: Section 3 lists the three stopping events and assigns direct evaluation to small K, Euler-Maclaurin to bK<1, and one last non-cubic transformation plus FFT precomputation to failure of |cK^2|<=0.01b. Section 4 separately dispatches near-boundary cubic coefficients to FFT data, nonstationary outer intervals to Euler-Maclaurin and quadratic sums, recursively shortens the central quadratic factor, treats failure of the new length condition termwise, and reserves the remaining stationary branch for Section 4.3.
nonparaphrase_operation: Reorganizes the case analysis by the invariant that fails and maps each failure to the representation that makes it cheap, showing that the exits collectively complete rather than interrupt the algorithm.
limits: Every route depends on the paper's parameter inequalities, precision convention, auxiliary lemmas, and prior quadratic evaluator. Several boundary reductions are described as tedious or delegated, so this is an architecture of certified routes rather than a standalone implementation or practicality claim.
quality_reason: Multiple parent units explicitly specify different halting conditions and distinct downstream methods. Their joint role is concrete and necessary to cover the parameter regimes, so the synthesis is more than a generic observation that algorithms use cases.

synthesis: For the bulk terms, extending the x-contour enables an exact Gaussian integration that converts each term into a one-dimensional cubic phase with an explicit saddle. Extracting that saddle and deforming the remaining contours separates computable boundary pieces, while decay of the saddle-phase coefficients allows its infinite expansion to be truncated into a finite polynomial-phase sum whose bounded coefficient ranges can be addressed by precomputed grid values.
source_support: Section 4.3 removes short endpoint tails, uses Lemma 5.6 to extend x to the full line, applies the Gaussian formula (4.29), defines the saddle y_k and phase coefficients d_s, and reduces the bulk to (4.40). Bound (4.36) makes the tail beyond S=3+floor(log N/log M) removable by Taylor expansion, yielding the finite sums (4.42)-(4.43); Section 4.4 then constructs the grid and FFT precomputation for that family.
nonparaphrase_operation: Composes contour geometry, saddle localization, coefficient decay, and discretization into a single compression map from a coupled analytic integral to a finite query family.
limits: The degree S and coefficient bounds depend on the stated N/M relation and parameter conditions. Endpoint and external-contour pieces rely on Lemmas 5.5 and 5.6, and grid addressability is an asymptotic evaluation claim rather than evidence of favorable numerical constants.
quality_reason: The parent units supply successive, explicit transformations: contour extension and Gaussian completion, saddle expansion with a quantified decaying tail, and grid-based evaluation of the resulting family. The synthesis neither invents a causal step nor suppresses the terminal parameter dependence.

synthesis: When the polynomial degree grows, gridding every higher phase coefficient independently overcounts the true family and breaches the desired precomputation budget. The stationary expansion instead expresses all coefficients above cubic through the shared parameters tau, rho, and gamma; together with the first three phase coefficients this gives a six-parameter function W whose local derivatives support a much sparser interpolation grid and restore the target FFT cost.
source_support: The independent formulation (4.54) is controlled only in the range R/9<=n<=R and has degree at most 12 there; for n<R/9 the source says direct evaluation gives only the weaker t^(37/117+o(1)) result and that treating many beta variables independently is costly. Equations (4.60)-(4.63) derive beta_(s+3)=tau eta_s(rho,gamma), and (4.64)-(4.66) use six-variable Cauchy and Taylor bounds before counting O(nu^2 M N^3) FFT work per tuple and an overall cost within O(Lambda^5 K^(4mu)).
nonparaphrase_operation: Uses algebraic dependence among apparently separate phase coefficients to quotient a growing-dimensional grid down to its generating parameters, then translates that reduced dimension into the recovered complexity bound.
limits: The six-parameter relation is specific to the saddle-phase expansion and its bounds; it does not establish universal low-dimensional structure. The derivative recovery is described as laborious and the result is asymptotic, not a numerical-practicality guarantee.
quality_reason: One parent exposes the failure mode of independent discretization, while the other derives the shared generators and quantifies the reduced grid cost. Their conjunction supports both the mechanism and its computational consequence.

synthesis: The auxiliary lemmas close the cost proof as a staged certification pipeline: Euler-Maclaurin first replaces a cubic sum by an integral plus derivative corrections; recursive derivative bounds make the correction depth logarithmic; frequency splitting reduces those corrections to quadratic sums; nonstationary contour deformation supplies decay and truncation; saddle-aware branches reduce the remaining integrals to Airy-type or incomplete-Gamma forms; and external contour tails return to the quadratic-sum endpoint.
source_support: Lemma 5.1 gives the Euler-Maclaurin decomposition, and Lemma 5.2 proves via the polynomial recursion (5.4) that M=ceil(8log(K/epsilon)) controls its remainder. Lemma 5.3 splits by |tau+alpha k| and reduces both frequency regions to quadratic sums. Lemma 5.4 deforms nonstationary contours to exponentially decaying directions. Lemma 5.5 separates stationary and nonstationary geometry and reduces to (5.27), Airy-type integrals, and incomplete Gamma evaluations. Lemma 5.6 controls the extended contour pieces and reduces their bulk and corrections to quadratic exponential sums handled by Theorem 2.1.
nonparaphrase_operation: Orders six lemmas by the proof burden discharged at each interface and shows that each analytic representation hands a finite, certified residue to the next established evaluator.
limits: The pipeline proves the stated conditional reductions and asymptotic costs, not optimized constants or numerical practicality. It imports Theorem 2.1 and earlier saddle procedures, and dense contour phases and normalizations are extraction-sensitive, so the synthesis avoids reconstructing exact signs or constants beyond the legible claims.
quality_reason: The parents jointly form an explicit dependency chain rather than a list of thematically related techniques: derivative control justifies truncation, separate geometric regimes justify different contour treatments, and all terminal residues are routed to named evaluators. The source remains sufficiently legible for this procedural claim despite formula-level OCR risk.
